title: Feed my sheep (John 21:15–19)
hookLine: three times: do you love me? feed my lambs
carry: the wound is opened, gently, so it can heal
tomorrow: John close: all the books in the world

lines: THREE DENIALS, NOT YET SPOKEN OF.
cards: Breakfast is over. The fish bones are on the coals. Peter is still sitting by the charcoal fire, the one that echoes the courtyard fire where he said, I am not.
Three times. John never tells us anyone has spoken of it since. Now Jesus turns to him, in front of the others, and asks him a question.
Then again. Then a third time. Everyone at that fire can count.

teach.h: SIMON, SON OF JONAS: THE OLD NAME.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs." Notice the name. Not Peter, the rock.
Simon, son of Jonas: the name he had before any of this began. A second time: lovest thou me? Yes, Lord.

teach.h: THE THIRD TIME, AND PETER IS GRIEVED.
teach.b: Then a third, and John says: "Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me?" He knows what three means. This time Peter doesn't argue or boast as he did at the supper.
He says: "Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee." You know everything, including that night. And each answer is not a lecture.
Three denials, three questions, three commissions. The wound is opened, gently, so it can heal. You may hear sermons on the Greek words for love here.
Jesus asks twice with agapao and once with phileo; Peter answers each time with phileo. Some readers see a deep difference.
Many scholars note that John uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere, so the shift may be style more than meaning. Churches read this commission differently.
Catholics see Peter's special role as chief shepherd of the whole church, which they believe passes to the popes.
Orthodox and Protestant Christians honor Peter's restoration, and many hear a calling for every pastor and every believer.
Then Jesus tells Peter that one day he'll be led where he doesn't want to go, and says the two words that have run through the whole story: follow me.

how: Many churches read this passage at ordinations of priests and pastors, and Catholics read it on feasts of Saint Peter, linking it with the ministry of the pope.

o: to fish with a wide net
to forgive a debt in full
to feed or graze a flock

games.q: what's inside John 21:15–19 — tap the pairs.
p: the last words of the scene

s: Jesus asks Peter the same question three times
three times: lovest thou me? three denials, three commissions.
scholars all agree the switch between agapao and phileo changes the meaning
many note that John uses the two verbs interchangeably elsewhere.
Jesus answers Peter's yes with a lecture about his failure
each time he answers with a job: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep.

games.q: you're Peter. you denied him three times. now he's asked you the third time: do you love me? what do you say?
o: of course I do. I'd die for you.
Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.
games.why: no boasting this time: "Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee." and the answer: "Feed my sheep."

practice: Think of someone in your life who's a sheep without much tending right now, overlooked, tired, new, lonely or a little lost, and picture their face.
What would feeding them look like: a meal, a call, help with a task, an hour of your attention? If you pray, hear the question asked of you, gently, and answer it with that one thing.
